title: Sleep
description: Class 20 practice: circadian rhythms and sleep hormones, the stages of sleep, what affects sleep, sleep across the lifespan, assessing sleep, sleep hygiene teaching, and the effects of poor sleep and shift work, for the Final Exam.

insomnia.intro: A nurse at a primary care clinic is seeing a client who reports trouble sleeping for 3 months.

tabs.title: Nurse's Notes
tabs.html:
Nurse's Notes

52-year-old office worker. Says, “I'm exhausted. I lie awake for hours, and I wake up around 3 a.m. and can't get back to sleep.” Company has announced layoffs; client says, “I can't stop thinking about it at night.” Vital signs within normal limits. No pain. Takes no prescribed medications.

tabs.title: Sleep Diary
tabs.html:
Sleep diary: typical weekday

TimeEntry
1500Coffee, 1 large cup
170020-minute walk
1900Coffee with dinner
21002 glasses of wine “to relax”
2130A few crackers
2230In bed; scrolls phone until about 0030
0300Awake about 1 hour
0600Alarm; gets up

Weekends: sleeps until 1000; 2-hour nap on Saturday.

questions.stem: A client asks why the nurse suggests dimming the lights and putting screens away an hour before bed. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?
options: “Darkness lowers cortisol, which is at its highest at bedtime.”
“Dim light raises serotonin, which keeps the brain more alert.”
“Darkness lets your body release melatonin, which signals sleep.”
“Darkness slows growth hormone, so the body is able to rest.”
questions.rationale:
Melatonin is the hormone of darkness: its secretion starts in the evening as light fades (around 2100 on the class's circadian clock) and stops in the morning. Bright light, including screens, holds it back, so dimming lights lets it rise.

Cortisol is the tempting choice, since it does follow a daily rhythm, but it's lowest around bedtime and rises toward morning, not the reverse. Serotonin promotes calm and relaxation (the reason for a light carbohydrate snack), not alertness, and growth hormone is released mostly during deep sleep, not slowed by darkness.

Takeaway: Darkness turns melatonin on and light turns it off; protect the evening from bright light.

questions.stem: A nurse who just started working night shifts asks how to fall asleep more easily after getting home in the morning. Which advice fits how light affects the body clock?
options: Wear dark sunglasses on the drive home, and darken the bedroom
Sit in bright morning sunlight for an hour, then go to sleep
Keep the bedroom bright so the body adjusts to sleeping in daylight
Take a long walk outdoors in the morning light before going to bed
questions.rationale:
Light is the strongest cue that sets the circadian clock, and morning light pushes the body toward wakefulness. A night worker who wants to sleep in the morning blocks light on the way home and sleeps in a dark room, so the clock isn't told it's daytime.

A long walk in the morning light is the tempting choice, because exercise and fresh air sound healthy, but morning light is exactly the cue that wakes the clock up. Sitting in sunlight does the same, and a bright bedroom keeps signaling day.

Takeaway: Light tells the body it's time to be awake; to sleep in the daytime, keep the light out.

questions.stem: A nurse caring for a client overnight finds an oral temperature of 36.3° C (97.3° F) at 0430. At 1900 the evening before, it was 37.0° C (98.6° F). The client is resting comfortably and has no other changes. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Apply a warming blanket and recheck it in 30 minutes
Report it to the provider as a sign of hypothermia
Recheck the temperature with a different thermometer
Document it as an expected daily variation
questions.rationale:
Body temperature follows a circadian rhythm: it's lowest in the early morning (around 0430) and highest in the early evening (around 1900). A drop of less than 1° C between those times, in a comfortable client with no other changes, is expected.

Rechecking with a different thermometer is the tempting choice, because a careful nurse confirms unexpected readings, but this one isn't unexpected; the value is normal and matches the daily low. A warming blanket and a report of hypothermia treat a normal value as a problem.

Takeaway: Temperature, heart rate, blood pressure, and hormones rise and fall on a 24-hour rhythm; compare readings with the time of day.

questions.stem: A client says she reads on a bright tablet in bed until about 0100, can't fall asleep before then, and struggles to get up at 0630 for work. Which teaching should the nurse give first?
options: Sleep later on weekends to make up the lost sleep
Turn off screens at least an hour before bedtime
Take a nap after work to make up for the short night
Have a glass of wine in the evening to help her relax
questions.rationale:
Light late in the evening easily nudges the circadian clock later (a delay), and a bright screen in bed also keeps the brain alert. Removing that light is the change that lets her sleep start earlier, so it comes first.

Sleeping later on weekends is the tempting choice, because she truly is short on sleep, but irregular wake times shift the clock even later and make Monday worse. A nap after work makes it harder to fall asleep at night, and wine makes sleep worse in the second half of the night.

Takeaway: Evening light pushes the body clock later; dim screens and lights well before bed, and keep wake times regular.

questions.stem: A client who has trouble falling asleep asks the nurse about a bedtime snack. Which snack should the nurse suggest?
options: A mug of hot cocoa
A few whole-grain crackers
A large bowl of chili
Leftover pepperoni pizza
questions.rationale:
A light carbohydrate snack before bed affects brain serotonin levels, which promotes calmness and relaxation. A few crackers fits.

Hot cocoa is the tempting choice, because a warm drink at bedtime sounds soothing, but chocolate contains caffeine, a stimulant. Chili and pepperoni pizza are heavy, spicy, and fatty: heavy meals within about 3 hours of bed disturb sleep.

Takeaway: Before bed: a light carbohydrate snack (it raises serotonin), not caffeine and not a heavy meal.

questions.stem: The parent of a 14-year-old who stays up late gaming asks why deep sleep matters while the teen is still growing. Which response by the nurse is accurate?
options: “Melatonin made during deep sleep builds bone and muscle.”
“Growth hormone is released mainly during REM sleep.”
“Cortisol peaks in deep sleep to help the body repair.”
“Most growth hormone is released during deep sleep.”
questions.rationale:
Growth hormone is released mostly during deep, slow-wave (NREM stage III and IV) sleep, early in the night. Too little sleep can suppress growth, one of the effects of missing sleep shown in class.

REM sleep is the tempting choice, because REM is often called the most important sleep, but REM's job is mental and emotional balance; growth hormone belongs to deep NREM sleep. Melatonin signals sleep timing, it doesn't build tissue, and cortisol rises toward morning, not in deep sleep.

Takeaway: Deep slow-wave sleep is when most growth hormone is released; REM supports the mind and emotions.

questions.stem: During a sleep study, a client is relaxed but still aware of the room, has a sudden jerk of one leg, and wakes at once when the technician speaks softly. Which stage of sleep is the client most likely in?
options: NREM stage II
NREM stage IV
NREM stage I
REM sleep
questions.rationale:
NREM stage I is the transition between wakefulness and sleep: the person is relaxed but aware, may have involuntary muscle jerks, is easily aroused, and stays there only minutes (about 5% of sleep).

Stage II is the tempting choice, since it's also light and the person can be aroused with relative ease, but in stage II the person has fallen asleep and is no longer aware of the surroundings. Stage IV is the deepest sleep, with difficult arousal, and REM sleep is hard to wake from, with large muscles nearly paralyzed.

Takeaway: Aware, jerking, and wakes instantly: stage I, the doorway between waking and sleep.

questions.stem: At 0200, a nurse has trouble waking a client who fell asleep at 2300. The client's heart rate is 58/min (72/min at bedtime), respirations are 12/min, and the client is slow to respond, then oriented and back to baseline within a minute. Which explanation fits these findings?
options: The client was in REM sleep, which slows the heart
The client was in NREM stage I, the lightest sleep
The client was in NREM stage II, the longest stage
The client was in the deepest stage of NREM sleep
questions.rationale:
NREM stage IV (delta, slow-wave sleep) is the greatest depth of sleep: temperature, heart rate, respirations, blood pressure, and metabolism all decrease, and arousal is difficult. A client who is slow to rouse, then fully oriented, fits this.

REM sleep is the tempting choice, because REM is also hard to wake from, but in REM the pulse becomes rapid and irregular and blood pressure rises or fluctuates; it doesn't slow. Stage I and stage II are light sleep, from which a client is aroused easily.

Takeaway: Slow vital signs and hard to wake: deep NREM (stage IV). Fast, irregular vital signs and hard to wake: REM.

questions.stem: A nurse checks on a sleeping client and sees the eyes darting under the closed lids, small twitches of the face, and irregular breathing with a faster pulse than earlier, while the arms and legs are limp. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Wake the client, and assess for signs of a seizure
Let the client sleep, since these are expected findings
Raise the head of the bed, and apply oxygen by cannula
Count the respirations for a minute, and call the provider
questions.rationale:
These are the findings of REM sleep: rapid eye movements, small muscle twitching (as on the face), large muscle immobility resembling paralysis, irregular respirations, and a rapid or irregular pulse. They're expected, so the nurse lets the client sleep.

Waking the client to assess for a seizure is the tempting choice, because twitching and irregular breathing can look worrying, but a seizure doesn't leave the large muscles limp, and waking the client takes away REM sleep. Oxygen and calling the provider treat normal REM findings as an emergency.

Takeaway: Darting eyes, facial twitches, irregular breathing, a faster pulse, and limp limbs: REM sleep, which is expected.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a group of students about REM sleep. Which findings should the nurse include as expected during REM sleep?
options: Rapid or irregular pulse
The slowest brain waves of the night
Blood pressure that rises or fluctuates
Large muscles nearly immobile
The lowest metabolic rate of the night
Increased gastric secretions
questions.rationale:
REM sleep is an active state: the pulse is rapid or irregular, blood pressure rises or fluctuates, gastric secretions increase, metabolism increases, the EEG is active, and the large muscles are nearly paralyzed.

The lowest metabolic rate is the tempting choice, because the body is so still in REM, but the lowest metabolism, along with the slowest brain waves, belongs to deep NREM stage IV. In REM, metabolism and brain activity rise.

Takeaway: REM: the brain and the heart are busy while the large muscles are still. Deep NREM: everything slows.

questions.stem: A client in the intensive care unit has been woken every hour for vital signs for 3 nights and is now irritable, anxious, and having trouble concentrating. The client's condition is now stable. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Ask the provider for a sleeping pill at bedtime
Keep the lights on so the client stays oriented
Group the care to allow 90-minute blocks of sleep
Leave the TV on low to give a familiar sound
questions.rationale:
Being woken every hour prevents full sleep cycles, which last about 90 minutes. REM periods come late in each cycle, so the client loses REM sleep, which is essential to mental and emotional equilibrium: irritability, anxiety, and poor concentration follow. Grouping care so the stable client gets uninterrupted 90-minute blocks restores full cycles.

A sleeping pill is the tempting choice, because the client clearly needs sleep, but sleep medications are a last resort, and they don't fix hourly waking. Lights on and the TV on add the light and noise that disturb sleep in the hospital.

Takeaway: Protect full 90-minute sleep cycles by clustering care; constant waking costs REM sleep and emotional balance.

questions.stem: A nursing student says, “Most of the night is spent in deep sleep.” Which correction by the nurse educator is accurate?
options: “About half of sleep is light NREM stage II sleep.”
“About half of sleep is spent in REM sleep.”
“About half of sleep is in the deepest NREM stage.”
“About half of sleep is the stage I transition.”
questions.rationale:
NREM stage II makes up about 50% to 55% of total sleep. Stage I is about 5%, stages III and IV about 10% each, and REM about 20% to 25%.

REM is the tempting choice, because REM is the best-known stage, but it's only about a fifth to a quarter of the night. The deepest stage is about 10%, and stage I lasts only minutes.

Takeaway: Stage II is about half of sleep, REM about a quarter, and the deepest stages and stage I much less.

questions.stem: A student usually sleeps from 2300 to 0700, but sets an alarm for 0430 the week before finals to study. Which part of the night's sleep is the student losing the most of?
options: REM sleep, which grows longer near morning
Deep NREM sleep, which grows longer near morning
Stage I sleep, which starts each of the sleep cycles
Stage II sleep, which mostly comes early in the night
questions.rationale:
Sleep cycles change through the night: deep NREM sleep is concentrated in the first cycles, while REM periods get longer as morning approaches. Cutting the end of the night therefore cuts a disproportionate amount of REM sleep, the sleep tied to memory and emotional balance.

Deep NREM sleep is the tempting choice, since deep sleep feels like the most important, but it comes mostly early in the night and is largely kept. Stage I lasts only minutes per cycle, and stage II is spread across the whole night.

Takeaway: Deep sleep comes early in the night and REM comes late, so cutting the morning short costs REM.

questions.stem: A client says, “A couple of drinks in the evening help me fall asleep.” Which response by the nurse is accurate?
options: “It's fine for sleep as long as you stop drinking an hour before bed.”
“It can make you drowsy, but it breaks up sleep later in the night.”
“It gives deeper sleep overall, though it may cause a headache.”
“It keeps helping your sleep as long as the amount stays the same.”
questions.rationale:
Alcohol may help people fall asleep, but it leads to poor-quality sleep in the second half of the night and less deep sleep overall. People also become tolerant to its sedating effect and drink more to get the same result.

Keeping the amount the same is the tempting choice, because a steady dose sounds controlled, but tolerance means the same amount helps less over time. Stopping an hour before bed is too close (the class teaches at least 4 hours), and alcohol gives less deep sleep, not more.

Takeaway: Alcohol helps you fall asleep but wrecks the second half of the night, and tolerance builds.

questions.stem: A client who smokes two packs of cigarettes a day says he wakes up every few hours during the night. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: “Smoking deepens sleep, so your waking has another cause.”
“Nicotine from the last cigarette keeps you in REM sleep.”
“Smoking lowers your oxygen level, so you stay in light sleep.”
“Nicotine wears off overnight, and the withdrawal disturbs sleep.”
questions.rationale:
Heavy smokers tend to sleep very lightly, have less REM sleep, and wake every 3 to 4 hours because of nicotine withdrawal. That's the likely cause of this client's waking.

Lower oxygen is the tempting choice, because smoking does harm the lungs, but the class's explanation for the regular waking is nicotine withdrawal. Smoking makes sleep lighter, not deeper, and it reduces REM sleep.

Takeaway: Heavy smoking means light sleep, less REM, and waking every 3 to 4 hours from withdrawal.

questions.stem: A hospitalized client slept poorly last night. Which factors may be contributing?
options: A light carbohydrate snack at 2100
Alarms from the roommate's IV pump during the night
Pain from an abdominal incision
A warm bath 90 minutes before bedtime
Worry about biopsy results due tomorrow
A diuretic given at 2000
questions.rationale:
Factors that affect sleep include the environment (noise above all: alarms), illness, pain, and medications (an incision; a diuretic in the evening causes nighttime urination), and psychological stress (worry about results).

The carbohydrate snack is the tempting choice, because eating near bedtime can disturb sleep, but a light carbohydrate snack is recommended: it raises serotonin. A warm bath 90 minutes before bed is also on the class's sleep hygiene list.

Takeaway: Look for noise, pain, medications, and worry; a light carbohydrate snack and a bath 90 minutes before bed help sleep.

questions.stem: A client with arthritis says that hip pain wakes her every night at about 0200. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Ask the provider for a sleeping medication
Give the analgesic when she wakes at 0200
Give the prescribed analgesic at bedtime
Teach her to avoid taking naps during the day
questions.rationale:
When pain is likely to interrupt sleep, the nurse gives the analgesic before bedtime, so relief is in place before the pain wakes her.

Giving it when she wakes is the tempting choice, because it treats the pain when it happens, but by then her sleep is already broken. A sleeping medication doesn't treat pain and is a last resort, and avoiding naps doesn't address what wakes her.

Takeaway: If pain is likely to wake the client, give the analgesic before bed.

questions.stem: A nurse has taught a client about caffeine and sleep. Which statement by the client shows understanding?
options: “I'll have my last cup of coffee by early afternoon.”
“A cola with dinner is fine, since it isn't coffee.”
“Coffee doesn't affect me, so one after dinner is fine.”
“I'll switch my after-dinner coffee to hot cocoa.”
questions.rationale:
Caffeine is a stimulant, and clients should avoid it for at least 4 to 6 hours before bed. Stopping by early afternoon leaves plenty of time.

Hot cocoa is the tempting choice, because it seems like a swap away from coffee, but chocolate has caffeine too, as does cola. Feeling that coffee "doesn't affect me" doesn't mean it doesn't disturb sleep quality.

Takeaway: Stop caffeine (coffee, tea, cola, chocolate) at least 4 to 6 hours before bed.

questions.stem: A nurse is preparing a hospitalized client for sleep. Which action best promotes sleep?
options: Leave the door open so staff can hear if the client calls
Leave the TV on low so the room doesn't feel too quiet
Offer the PRN sleeping medication at bedtime each night
Close the door, dim the lights, and group nighttime care
questions.rationale:
Noise and light are major environmental barriers to sleep in the hospital. Closing the door, dimming lights, and grouping care reduce both, and grouping care allows longer stretches of sleep.

Leaving the door open is the tempting choice, because staff want to hear the client, but the call light serves that purpose, and hallway noise keeps the client awake. The TV adds light and sound, and a sleeping medication every night isn't a first step.

Takeaway: In the hospital: dark, quiet, door closed, and care grouped to protect sleep.

questions.stem: A client having surgery in the morning can't sleep and asks the nurse for something to help. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Give the PRN sleeping medication that is prescribed
Ask the client what's on her mind about the surgery
Bring a warm drink, and turn down the room lights
Explain that most people don't sleep well before surgery
questions.rationale:
Psychological stress is a common cause of poor sleep, and the nurse assesses before acting. Asking what's on her mind finds the cause and may relieve it.

A warm drink and dim lights is the tempting choice, because both are comforting, but they skip assessing the worry that is keeping her awake. The sleeping medication is a last resort, and explaining that it's common dismisses her concern.

Takeaway: When stress keeps a client awake, assess the worry first; medications are a last resort.

questions.stem: A client says he gets up three times a night to urinate. Which teaching should the nurse give?
options: Cut the total fluid intake for the day by about half
Drink most fluids earlier, and cut back 2 to 4 hours before bed
Drink a full glass of water just before going to bed
Take the prescribed diuretic with dinner instead of breakfast
questions.rationale:
The class teaches decreasing fluid intake 2 to 4 hours before bed. Moving fluids earlier keeps daily intake adequate while cutting nighttime urination.

Cutting total fluids in half is the tempting choice, because less fluid means less urine, but it risks dehydration. A full glass at bedtime fills the bladder overnight, and a diuretic with dinner works through the night.

Takeaway: Keep total fluids up, but drink most of them earlier in the day, cutting back 2 to 4 hours before bed.

questions.stem: A first-time parent worries that their 3-week-old sleeps about 18 hours a day, and that the baby's eyes move and face twitches during sleep. Which response by the nurse is accurate?
options: “At 3 weeks, babies should be awake about half the day.”
“The twitching suggests the baby's sleep is too light.”
“Most babies sleep through the night by 3 weeks of age.”
“Newborns sleep most of the day, much of it in REM sleep.”
questions.rationale:
Newborns and infants average 16 to 24 hours of sleep a day, and their sleep is mainly REM, with its eye movements and twitches. This baby's pattern is expected.

Twitching means the sleep is too light is the tempting choice, because the movements look restless, but they're signs of REM sleep, which makes up most of a newborn's sleep. Babies aren't awake half the day at 3 weeks, and they usually sleep through the night at about 8 to 16 weeks, not 3.

Takeaway: Newborns sleep 16 to 24 hours a day, mostly in REM.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old client says, “I sleep about 6 hours, wake up once or twice, and I'm up at 5 every morning. I must have insomnia.” The client feels rested during the day. Which response by the nurse is best?
options: “Those are common sleep changes that come with age.”
“You should still sleep about 8 hours, like a younger adult.”
“Waking during the night means you need a sleep study.”
“A sleeping pill can bring back the deep sleep you've lost.”
questions.rationale:
Older adults average 5 to 7 hours of sleep; their sleep is less sound, deep (stage IV) sleep is absent or much decreased, REM periods shorten, and they wake earlier. A client who feels rested during the day is getting enough.

Needing a sleep study is the tempting choice, because sleep complaints deserve attention, but these findings are expected for age and the client feels rested. Expecting 8 hours applies a younger adult's norm, and sleeping pills don't restore deep sleep and carry fall risks in older adults.

Takeaway: Older adults sleep less, wake more, rise earlier, and lose deep sleep; judge by how rested they feel.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a group of older adults about sleep. Which changes should the nurse describe as expected with aging?
options: More total hours of sleep
Less deep (stage IV) sleep
More time spent in REM sleep
More difficulty falling asleep
Deeper, sounder sleep overall
Waking up earlier in the morning
questions.rationale:
In older adults, stage IV sleep is absent or much decreased, sleep is less sound, REM periods shorten (so REM time doesn't grow), they have more difficulty falling asleep, and they arise earlier.

More total sleep is the tempting choice, because older adults may nap more or spend longer in bed, but average nighttime sleep is shorter (about 5 to 7 hours), and it's lighter, not sounder. More REM is also wrong: REM periods shorten with age.

Takeaway: With age: less deep sleep, shorter REM, harder to fall asleep, earlier waking, and fewer total hours.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old client says it takes longer to fall asleep than it used to, and she now notices every noise at night. Which response by the nurse is best?
options: “Those are signs of a sleep disorder that needs a sleep study.”
“Deep sleep increases at your age, so the noise isn't the cause.”
“Those changes are common in middle age; let's review your habits.”
“Most people need more sleep in their 40s than in their 20s.”
questions.rationale:
In middle-aged adults, time awake in bed increases (it takes longer to fall asleep), stage IV sleep decreases, and they become more aware of sleep disturbances. Reviewing her habits finds what she can change.

A sleep study is the tempting choice, because the complaints are real, but they match expected changes, and habits come first. Deep sleep decreases in middle age, which is why noise wakes her more, and sleep needs don't rise in the 40s.

Takeaway: Middle age: slower to fall asleep, less deep sleep, and more aware of disturbances.

questions.stem: The parent of a 4-year-old says bedtime has become a nightly struggle. Which teaching should the nurse give?
options: Let the child stay up until she falls asleep on her own
Let the child use a tablet in bed so she can wind down quietly
Give the child a long nap late in the afternoon instead
Keep the same routine each night: bath, teeth, then a story
questions.rationale:
A regular bedtime routine is especially important for children: a warm bath, brushing teeth, quiet music or a story, at the same time each night.

Letting her fall asleep on her own is the tempting choice, because it avoids the struggle, but it removes the regular bedtime that sets her body clock. A tablet in bed adds bright light and stimulation, and a late, long nap pushes bedtime later.

Takeaway: Children sleep best with the same bedtime and the same routine every night.

questions.stem: A client with trouble sleeping is asked to keep a sleep diary. Which instruction should the nurse give?
options: Record the hours of sleep on two typical nights
Record entries for 2 weeks on the nights you sleep badly
Record bedtime, time to fall asleep, and wakings for 2 weeks
Record how rested you feel each morning for a month
questions.rationale:
A sleep diary is a diagnostic tool kept for 14 days: the time to bed, the time it takes to fall asleep, the number and times of awakenings, wake time, total hours, food, drink, and medications, activities, and worries.

Recording only the bad nights is the tempting choice, because those are the problem, but the good nights show what helps. Two nights are too few to see a pattern, and how rested you feel alone leaves out the timing data.

Takeaway: A sleep diary covers every night for 14 days, with times, wakings, intake, activities, and worries.

questions.stem: A nurse is explaining what to include in a sleep diary. Which items should the client record?
options: The dreams remembered each morning
Foods, drinks, and medications, with their times
The client's blood pressure each morning
Activities in the 2 to 3 hours before bed
The number and times of awakenings
The client's weight each morning
questions.rationale:
The class's sleep diary includes the times of going to bed, falling asleep, waking at night, and waking in the morning; food, drink, and medications; physical and mental activities; activities 2 to 3 hours before bedtime, rituals, and changes in the environment; and worries or anxieties.

Remembered dreams is the tempting choice, because dreams feel connected to sleep, but they aren't part of the diary and don't show the patterns it looks for. Daily weight and blood pressure aren't part of it.

Takeaway: The diary tracks timing, intake, activities before bed, the environment, and worries.

questions.stem: A nurse is completing a sleep assessment. Which client response needs follow-up?
options: “I text and watch videos in bed until I fall asleep.”
“It takes me about 15 minutes to fall asleep at night.”
“I go to bed at 2230 and get up at 0630, weekends too.”
“On weekends I get up within an hour of my usual time.”
questions.rationale:
The sleep assessment asks whether the client reads, watches TV, texts, or eats in bed. Screens in bed add light and stimulation and teach the brain that bed is for being awake, so this needs follow-up and teaching.

Falling asleep in 15 minutes is the tempting choice, because the nurse is asking about time to fall asleep, but 15 minutes is well within the normal range. Regular bed and wake times, even on weekends, are good sleep hygiene.

Takeaway: Ask what the client does in bed; screens, work, and eating in bed need teaching.

questions.stem: A client says she naps for 2 hours every afternoon and then lies awake until 0200. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Explain that long naps delay sleep, and plan to shorten them
Suggest going to bed earlier to allow more time to fall asleep
Suggest staying in bed with eyes closed until sleep comes
Ask the provider about a sleeping medication at bedtime
questions.rationale:
Lengthy naps take away the sleep drive the client needs at night. The class teaches eliminating lengthy naps; a short nap, if any, is far less disruptive.

Going to bed earlier is the tempting choice, because it seems to give more time for sleep, but it means more time lying awake in bed. Staying in bed until sleep comes goes against the 20-minute rule, and medication is a last resort.

Takeaway: Long daytime naps steal night sleep; shorten or drop them before anything else.

questions.stem: A client says, “When I can't sleep, I lie in bed for hours watching the clock.” Which teaching should the nurse give?
options: Stay in bed with your eyes closed until you finally fall asleep
If you're awake after about 20 minutes, get up and do something dull
Watch TV in bed until you begin to feel drowsy, then turn it off
Get up and exercise until you feel tired enough to fall back asleep
questions.rationale:
Sleep hygiene says: if you can't sleep within 20 minutes, get up and do something boring, and return when sleepy. Lying awake teaches the brain that bed is for worrying.

Staying in bed with eyes closed is the tempting choice, because resting seems better than nothing, but it strengthens the link between bed and wakefulness. TV in bed breaks the rule that the bed is only for sleep, and exercise at night is stimulating.

Takeaway: Can't sleep in 20 minutes? Get up, do something boring, and go back when sleepy.

questions.stem: A client works on a laptop in bed each night and then has trouble falling asleep. Which change should the nurse suggest?
options: Turn the laptop's brightness down while working in bed
Stop the laptop work in bed an hour before turning off the lights
Work in bed sitting upright against pillows, not lying down
Do the laptop work in another room, and keep the bed for sleep
questions.rationale:
Sleep hygiene: use the bed only for sleep and sex. Moving the work out of the bed lets the bed become a cue for sleep again.

Stopping an hour before lights out is the tempting choice, because it removes the screen before sleep, but the bed is still where work happens. Dimming the screen and sitting upright also keep working in bed.

Takeaway: Keep the bed for sleep (and sex) only, so it becomes a cue for sleep.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a client who has trouble sleeping. Which instructions should the nurse include?
options: Get up at the same time each day, weekends included.
Get some sunlight early in the morning.
Avoid heavy meals in the 3 hours before bed.
Sleep in on weekends to catch up on lost sleep.
Take a warm bath about 90 minutes before bed.
Keep the bedroom quiet and comfortable.
questions.rationale:
The class's sleep hygiene teaching includes regular wake and bed times, morning sunlight to set the biological clock, avoiding heavy meals 3 hours before bed, a warm bath 90 minutes before bed, and a quiet, comfortable bedroom.

Sleeping in on weekends is the tempting choice, because it seems to repay the week's sleep debt, but it shifts the body clock later and makes Sunday and Monday nights harder.

Takeaway: Same times every day, light evenings, morning sunlight, a bath 90 minutes before bed, and a quiet bedroom; no weekend sleeping in.

questions.stem: On his first night in the hospital, a client asks for a sleeping pill. He says he never takes one at home. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Give the PRN sleeping medication as requested
Explain that sleeping pills are used as a last resort
Ask what usually helps him fall asleep at home
Offer to turn on the TV until he feels drowsy
questions.rationale:
Sleeping medications are a last resort, and the nurse assesses first. Asking what helps at home (a routine, a snack, reading, a pillow) lets the nurse recreate it in the hospital.

Explaining that pills are a last resort is the tempting choice, because it's true, but it tells him no without offering help or finding out what works for him. Giving the medication skips the nondrug measures, and the TV adds light and noise.

Takeaway: Before a sleeping pill, assess the client's usual routine and use nondrug measures first.

questions.stem: A client who runs at 2100 each night has trouble falling asleep. Which suggestion should the nurse make?
options: Move the run to the morning or afternoon
Run harder to be more tired at bedtime
Stop exercising until sleep gets better
Shorten the run to 15 minutes at 2100
questions.rationale:
Exercise helps sleep, but not close to bedtime: the class teaches stopping hours before bed. Moving the run earlier keeps the benefit without the stimulation.

A shorter run at 2100 is the tempting choice, because less exercise sounds less stimulating, but it's still right before bed. Running harder adds stimulation, and stopping exercise loses its benefits for sleep.

Takeaway: Keep exercising, but finish hours before bedtime.

questions.stem: A nurse has taught a client about sleep hygiene. Which statement by the client shows understanding?
options: “I'll sleep in on Saturdays to catch up from the week.”
“I'll take a long nap after work to recharge for the evening.”
“I'll have a small glass of wine at bedtime to help me relax.”
“I'll get up at the same time every morning, weekends too.”
questions.rationale:
Getting up and going to bed at the same time every day anchors the circadian clock and is a core sleep hygiene rule.

A small glass of wine is the tempting choice, because a small amount sounds harmless, but alcohol disrupts the second half of the night and should be avoided at least 4 hours before bed. Sleeping in and long naps both disrupt the schedule.

Takeaway: The same wake time every day, weekends included, is the anchor of sleep hygiene.

questions.topic: Effects of poor sleep and shift work
questions.stem: A nurse working three night shifts in a row asks how to sleep during the day. Which advice should the nurse give?
options: Stay up after the shift to run errands, then sleep in the afternoon
Make the bedroom dark and quiet, and keep the same sleep hours
Drink a large coffee at 0500 to stay alert for the drive home
Sleep with the TV on to block out daytime noise in the house
questions.rationale:
Daytime sleep after night shift needs the same hygiene as night sleep: a dark, quiet room and regular sleep hours, even when the shift moves sleep into the day.

Coffee at 0500 is the tempting choice, because staying alert on the drive home matters, but caffeine that late keeps the nurse from sleeping in the morning. Errands before sleep delay sleep and add morning light, and the TV adds light and sound.

Takeaway: Night workers protect daytime sleep with darkness, quiet, and a regular schedule.

questions.topic: Effects of poor sleep and shift work
questions.stem: A nurse is on the fourth 12-hour night shift in a row and feels very drowsy at 0400. The unit allows staff to rest on breaks. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Leave the charting until 0600, after the drowsiest time
Eat a large meal on the next break for more energy
Skip the break so the work will be finished early
Take a short nap or a brisk walk on the next break
questions.rationale:
Fatigue-related errors rise with consecutive night shifts and long hours. To stay alert, the class suggests napping on the job when allowed, staying active during breaks, and a caffeinated drink. A short nap or brisk walk is the safe step now.

Leaving the charting until 0600 is the tempting choice, because the nurse is trying to plan around drowsiness, but tedious tasks shouldn't be left for the end of the shift, when drowsiness peaks around 0400 to 0500 and continues. A large meal adds sluggishness, and skipping the break removes the chance to recover.

Takeaway: Drowsy on nights: nap or move on your break, and don't save tedious work for the end of the shift.

questions.topic: Effects of poor sleep and shift work
questions.stem: A client who works two jobs sleeps 4 to 5 hours a night. Which long-term health risks of short sleep should the nurse include in teaching?
options: Lower blood pressure
Type 2 diabetes
Faster reaction times
Obesity
Heart disease and stroke
A stronger immune response
questions.rationale:
Missing sleep raises the risk of type 2 diabetes, obesity, and heart disease and stroke, and it impairs the immune system.

Lower blood pressure is the tempting choice, because people think of sleep as rest for the heart, but short sleep raises cardiovascular risk. Sleep loss slows reaction time, and it weakens immunity rather than strengthening it.

Takeaway: Short sleep raises the risk of diabetes, obesity, heart disease and stroke, and infections.

questions.topic: Effects of poor sleep and shift work
questions.stem: After a night with very little sleep, a student says, “I feel fine, so I'm safe to drive home.” Which response by the nurse is accurate?
options: “Sleep loss slows your reactions, even when you feel alert.”
“If you feel alert, your reaction time has recovered.”
“It takes weeks of lost sleep to affect your driving.”
“A strong coffee will fully undo the effects of sleep loss.”
questions.rationale:
Short-term effects of sleep loss include increased reaction time, decreased accuracy, and cognitive impairment. Drowsy driving causes about 100,000 crashes a year, and feeling alert doesn't mean the effects are gone.

A strong coffee is the tempting choice, because caffeine does help alertness for a while, but it doesn't fully reverse the effects of lost sleep. Even one short night slows reactions, and feeling fine isn't a reliable sign of recovery.

Takeaway: Even one short night slows reaction time; feeling alert isn't proof of being safe.

questions.topic: Effects of poor sleep and shift work
questions.stem: A nurse finishing a 12-hour night shift nearly fell asleep at a red light on the way home last week. Which plan is safest for today's drive?
options: Open the car windows and play loud music
Drink a large coffee just before leaving
Take a short nap at work before driving home
Take a route with more traffic lights
questions.rationale:
Nurses on night and rotating shifts are much more likely to doze off driving home. When a nurse is too drowsy to drive safely, a short nap before driving treats the cause: the sleep debt.

A large coffee before leaving is the tempting choice, because caffeine is a recommended alertness tool on the job, but it doesn't make a drowsy driver safe, and it disrupts the day's sleep that follows. Open windows and loud music don't restore alertness, and a route with more lights adds stops where she nearly fell asleep.

Takeaway: Too drowsy to drive after a night shift? Nap first; tricks to stay awake don't make it safe.

questions.stem: Which entries in the sleep diary are likely contributing to the client's sleep problem?
options: A 20-minute walk at 1700
Coffee with dinner at 1900
Two glasses of wine at 2100
Scrolling the phone in bed
Sleeping until 1000 on weekends
A few crackers at 2130
questions.rationale:
Coffee at 1900 is caffeine within 4 hours of bed. Wine at 2100 breaks up sleep in the second half of the night, which fits waking at 0300. Phone use in bed adds light and keeps the bed linked to wakefulness. Sleeping until 1000 on weekends shifts the body clock.

The crackers are the tempting choice, because eating late can disturb sleep, but a light carbohydrate snack is recommended. A walk at 1700 is exercise well before bedtime, which helps sleep.

Takeaway: Read a sleep diary for caffeine and alcohol timing, screens in bed, and irregular wake times; light snacks and early exercise help.

questions.stem: In addition to sleep hygiene teaching, which action should the nurse take next?
options: Ask the provider about prescribing a sleeping medication
Explore the client's worries about work and ways to cope
Suggest a longer weekend nap to recover from the week
Suggest going to bed at 2100 to allow more time to sleep
questions.rationale:
The notes show psychological stress (the layoffs) keeping the client awake. Exploring the worries and ways to cope addresses a cause the hygiene teaching doesn't reach.

A sleeping medication is the tempting choice, because the client is exhausted after 3 months, but medications are a last resort, and the stress and habits come first. A longer nap worsens night sleep, and an earlier bedtime means more time awake in bed.

Takeaway: When worry keeps a client awake, address the stress along with the sleep habits.

questions.stem: Two weeks later, the client brings a new sleep diary. Which finding shows the plan is working?
options: Sleeps until 1100 on weekends to catch up
Takes a 2-hour nap on both Saturday and Sunday
Falls asleep within about 20 minutes on most nights
Has the wine at 2000 instead of at 2100
questions.rationale:
The goal is better sleep, and falling asleep within about 20 minutes on most nights shows the changes are working.

Wine at 2000 is the tempting choice, because it's an hour earlier, but it's still within 4 hours of bed, so it still disrupts sleep. Sleeping until 1100 and 2-hour naps are habits the plan was meant to change.

Takeaway: Evaluate with the sleep diary: faster sleep onset and fewer wakings show success; small shifts in bad habits don't.

questions.stem: A client who flew from California to Boston yesterday is wide awake at midnight Boston time and asks how to adjust. Which advice should the nurse give?
options: Get outside in the early morning sunlight there
Sleep late tomorrow to make up the lost hours
Keep the room dim for most of the next morning
Take a long nap tomorrow afternoon to catch up
questions.rationale:
Flying east means the body clock must move earlier. The clock is easily nudged in the advance direction by light in the early morning, so morning sunlight at the new location resets it fastest. The class's sleep hygiene list says it simply: use sunlight to set the biological clock.

Sleeping late is the tempting choice, because the client is short on sleep, but sleeping through the morning skips the light cue and keeps the client on California time. A dim morning does the same, and a long afternoon nap makes the next night harder.

Takeaway: Morning light moves the body clock earlier; evening light moves it later.

questions.stem: A client says, “Just as I'm dozing off, my leg jerks and I wake up feeling like I'm falling.” Which response by the nurse is accurate?
options: “That happens in REM sleep, while you're dreaming.”
“That happens in the deepest stage of your sleep.”
“That's common in the light first stage of sleep.”
“That means you skipped the lighter sleep stages.”
questions.rationale:
Involuntary muscle jerking is a feature of NREM stage I, the transition from wakefulness to sleep, when the person is easily aroused. It's common and harmless.

REM sleep is the tempting choice, because a falling feeling sounds like a dream, but in REM the large muscles are nearly paralyzed, and REM comes later in the cycle. The deepest stage is hard to wake from, and the jerk shows the client is in the lightest stage, not skipping it.

Takeaway: Jerks while drifting off happen in stage I, the lightest sleep.

questions.stem: The parent of a 5-week-old asks when the baby will sleep through the night. Which response by the nurse is accurate?
options: “Most babies do it by 5 weeks, so it should be soon.”
“Many babies start between about 2 and 4 months.”
“Most babies don't do it until they're a year old.”
“It usually starts once a baby eats solid foods.”
questions.rationale:
Each baby is different, but infants usually sleep through the night at about 8 to 16 weeks (2 to 4 months).

Starting solid foods is the tempting choice, because it's a popular belief, but it isn't what the class teaches, and most babies sleep through earlier. Five weeks is too early, and a year is much later than usual.

Takeaway: Babies usually begin sleeping through the night at about 8 to 16 weeks.

questions.topic: Effects of poor sleep and shift work
questions.stem: A college student who sleeps about 5 hours a night says, “I keep catching every cold that goes around.” Which response by the nurse is accurate?
options: “Short sleep mainly affects mood, so look for another cause.”
“Colds spread mostly to people who nap in the daytime.”
“Short sleep raises body temperature, which helps viruses.”
“Short sleep weakens the immune system over time.”
questions.rationale:
An impaired immune system is one of the effects of missing sleep, so frequent colds fit this student's short sleep.

Short sleep mainly affects mood is the tempting choice, because irritability is the most noticeable effect, but sleep loss affects the whole body, including immunity. Sleep loss tends to lower body temperature, and napping isn't a cause of colds.

Takeaway: Missing sleep weakens immunity, along with mood, memory, and metabolism.

questions.stem: A client says a streetlight shines into her bedroom and the room gets warm at night. Which suggestion should the nurse make?
options: Leave a lamp on low so the streetlight is less noticeable
Use room-darkening shades, and keep the room cool and quiet
Keep the TV on low to cover outside sounds and light
Sleep on the living room couch, where it's darker
questions.rationale:
The bedroom should be dark, quiet, and comfortable. Room-darkening shades block the light that suppresses melatonin, and a comfortable temperature helps sleep.

Sleeping on the couch is the tempting choice, because the room is darker, but it trades one problem for an uncomfortable bed and a room used for other activities. A lamp and the TV add more light.

Takeaway: Make the bedroom dark, quiet, and comfortable rather than working around light.

questions.stem: During a sleep assessment, a client says, “I nap sometimes.” Which question should the nurse ask next?
options: “Do you feel tired in the afternoons?”
“Have you been someone who naps for years?”
“How often do you nap, and for how long?”
“Do your naps help you feel better?”
questions.rationale:
The class's sleep assessment asks about naps: how often and how long. Frequency and length decide whether naps help or interfere with night sleep.

Whether the naps help is the tempting choice, because it asks about the client's experience, but a long nap can feel good and still ruin the night. Being tired in the afternoon and always napping don't give the facts the nurse needs.

Takeaway: For naps, assess how often and how long.
